## Discussion

<!-- P1: Opening paragraph -->
This study aimed to compare muscle mass and strength accretion in healthy young and old individuals that exercised with a low and moderate training volume for 10 weeks. In addition, secondary aims were to provide insight into the effects of said intervention on ribosome biogenesis and glucose tolerance. Overall, both young and old participants in the intervention responded in terms of muscle growth and -strength, also improving their tolerance to glucose ingestion. There was weak to strong evidence that the young participants had a larger gain in measures of muscle mass compared to old, but this was mostly limited to muscle mass measurements. In terms of low vs. moderate condition, both young and old had clear benefits of a moderate training volume in muscle volume, but this was less clear in muscle thickness for the young. In upper-body lean mass, young clearly increased following both doses, but there were only weak/uncertain evidence of the same for old. In strength however, the young responded better to low vs. moderate volume at all angular velocities of isometric and isokinetic peak torque and bicep curl MVC, with no difference in 1RM. The old showed no clear dose difference in strength measures apart from bicep curl MVC, where moderate-volume training was favoured. There was however a clear and credible difference between young and old regarding their glucose tolerance, where young improved more than the old. Both young and old intervention groups increased content of total RNA, though at different times (young at week 3, old at post), UBF and c-Myc, however old control also increased content of UBF. Lastly, the RNA-seq data showed a clear difference between young and old at baseline, which turned remarkably similar after training. 

<!-- P2: Hypertrophy and strength -->

<!-- POINT 1: General expectations in young and old when exercising resistance training -->
While it has been suggested that older adults can gain similar improvements in both muscle mass and -strength as young [FRAGALA19], this was not clearly evident in the present study. The young participants had larger gains from pre to post in thigh muscle volume and upper-body lean mass, with some weaker evidence of the same for muscle thickness, compared to the old. However, this was not true for muscle strength, where young and old had largely similar pre to post changes across the board. Hypertrophy attenuation in older individuals (~60+ years) is a broadly used statement [BETZ25, ENDO20, STEC17], likely stemming from the classic MRI CSA study by Welle and co-workers [WELLE96], where they found that older individuals (62-72yrs) experienced lesser training-induced increases in skeletal muscle CSA in the elbow and knee flexors compared to young. However, Welle et al. also found no difference in skeletal muscle CSA between young and old in the knee extensors. In terms of strength, older individuals increased similarly to young in elbow flexors and knee extensors, and in fact surpassed young in knee flexor strength, when strength was analysed as relative change in specific tension (strength per cm2 of CSA) [WELLE96]. Based on this, while hypertrophy attenuation was present in certain skeletal muscle, it was not universal, and despite less hypertrophy, older individuals had similar and even larger gains in specific tension strength [WELLE96]. An important point here, was that hypertrophy was not universal to all skeletal muscle groups, and a later work by Greig et al. [GREIG2011] noted that the litteratur was quite equivocal on this topic, either finding skeletal muscle mass in old to be less responsive [WELLE96, KOSEK06] or similar to young [IVEY00]. Furthermore, recent work find no decline in the potential for muscle hypertrophy [KARLSEN20] or no substantial influence of age on muscle hypertrophy response to resistance training [DE SANTANA24]. Among the studies that have compared young and old head-to-head to this date, the results are inconclusive at best, with some finding less myofiber hypertrophy in old compared to young [PETRELLA06, KOSEK06], less myofiber hypertrophy but similar strength gains [BICKEL11, RAUE09], or less myofiber hypertrophy and strength after 10.5 weeks, where muscle strength caught up after 21 weeks [MERO13]. Taken together, most studies measuring hypertrophy in knee extensors via whole-muscle volume MRI find no age effect [WELLE96, IVEY00, KARLSEN20, DE SANTANA24], with the exceptions being the findings of Raue et al. [RAUE09] and Welle and co-workers data on knee and elbow flexors [WELLE96]. When hypertrophy is measured on the fiber level though, this flips, and most studies find an attenuation in old compared to young [KOSEK06, PETRELLA06, BICKEL11, MERO13], the exception here being Karlsen et al. (2020). In this regard, our data does not show a definitive age effect on training-induced hypertrophy, though the moderate-to-strong evidence that thigh muscle volume and upper-body lean mass increased more in young compared to old does indicate that an age effect was more likely than not.

While there was moderate evidence of an age effect on muscle hypertrophy, there was none for muscle strength, which lines up well with previous findings where old individuals may lag behind in hypertrophy but not in strength [WELLE96, BICKEL11, MERO13] or where both change similarly [RAUE09]. The most common explanation for a discrepancy between skeletal muscle hypertrophy and -strength, is that neural adaptation drives the early stage strength gain, while hypertrophy is lagging behind [SOURCES]. This does not fully apply here, since both young and old had gains in muscle mass and -strength, only the young had larger gains in muscle mass than old. Therefore, the old participants in the present study effectively gained similar increases in strength, with less changes in muscle mass, indeed corroborating that hypertrophy and strength does not have a 1:1 relationship. This was addressed previously by Reggiani and Schiaffino [REGGIANI20], arguing that there are three possible relationships between size change and strength change; strength can increase in proportion to, less or more than size. At the core of this concept, lies the idea that not all muscle growth is forceful, where the proportion between sarcoplasmic proteins and myofibrillar proteins can be altered during hypertrophy, producing a higher or lower density of actual force-generating molecular motors per unit of muscle size [REGGIANI20]. Therefore, theres no given % of CSA, muscle volume, lean mass that grant a proportional increase in the contractile machinery, some of the gain could be sarcoplasmic rather than myofibrillar [REGGIANI20]. Alternatively or additionally, it could stem from myosin isoform shifts and post-translational changes to the contractile machinery, affecting force generation independent of size [REGGIANI20]. Notably, myofibrillar vs. sarcoplasmic hypertrophy, myosin isoform shifts and post-translational changes are less, if at all, explored in young vs. old participants, but the notion that the skeletal muscle mass can get stronger without the same growth in size at least seems like a plausible explanation for why the old in the present study increased similarly in strength, but not size, compared to the young. Further complicating this, is that the old control group also improved several strength measures, namely the 1RM leg press, isometric and isokinetic variables. Only the 1RM change in the control group could be categorized as credible and a strong effect, while the peak torque data showed moderate evidence of a real change (not credible) at the slowest angular velocity, which weakened with increasing angular velocities. One possible explanation for this could be the well-known learning effect [SORUCE], since the present study only had 1 familiarization test prior to pre testing. If that was the only explanation though, it does not make sense that the control group decreased their bicep curl MVC credibly from pre to post.<!-- probably need to discuss the control increase a bit more-->

<!-- POINT 2: Dose-response, low vs. moderate -->
In broad strokes, moderate-volume training was most beneficial in the hypertrophy outcomes (muscle volume, muscle thickness), for both age groups. However, looking at strength outcomes, there were more cases of low-volume training being more beneficial (peak torque, bicep curl MVC) for the young, while the old either show no difference (peak torque) or a benefit from moderate over low-volume training (bicep curl MVC). In terms of 1RM leg press and upper-body lean mass, we saw no evidence of a difference in either age group. Most studies investigating the effects of training volume on muscle mass and/or -strength, tend to find that a moderate-training volume benefits both size and strength [KRIEGER09/10,  HAMMARSTROM20, ROCHA23,CHEN23, LIXANDRAO24], where Hammarström et al. demonstrated that young benefited more from a moderate volume in both muscle mass and strength, a contrast to our findings that low-volume training was more beneficial.<!-- maybe comment this further--> A similar pattern to the present study was observed by Da Silva et al. [DA SILVA18], where more training volume improved hypertrophy compared to low, but no additional gain in strength/neuromuscular outcomes. Da Silva et al. (2018) notably only had old participants, and the volume manipulation was done through one group performing repetitions to failure, two groups performing submaximal repetitions, one of which doubled the amount of sets the repetitions to failure group had.<!-- maybe comment this further --> Further, a recent mate-regression by Pelland et al. [PELLAND24] found a clear positive effect of volume on both hypertrophy and strength <!-- both young and old? --> (posterior probability of 100%), but also deminishing returns in both, where he diminishing returns for strength was considerably more pronounced than for hypertrophy. As such, it seems hypertrophy could be more volume-sensitive than strength, with some evidence of strength not always following hypertrophy after increasing training volume [PELLAND24]. This could be corroborated by that strength saturates at a much lower training dose, as seen when comparing Schoenfeld et al. (2017), where volume reached a significant effect on hypertrophy at 10+ sets/week, against Krieger (2009), where strength gains only required 2-3 sets per session. Also of interest, Schoenfeld [SCHOENFELD17] found the opposite pattern when manipulating training load rather than volume, where strength was clearly load dependent and hypertophy insensitive. Furthermore, in 2019, Schoenfeld recruited 34 resistance-trained men randomized to low-volume, moderate-volum, or high-volume training, and found that while all groups experienced similar gains in muscle strength and endurance, muscle hypertrophy significantly increased with higher training volumes [SCHOENFELD19]. Thus, one could argue that the this field is quite equivocal, but that may very well stem from the wide spread in study designs. 

Many of the aforementioned studies differ in population or duration, manipulate volume or intensity differently, or investigate old and young separately. The two studies including both young and old differ substantially in design, where one first implemented a volume/dose model in the maintenance phase [BICKEL11], while the other manipulated training intensity rather than training volume [LETOCART21]. Bickel et al. (2011) recruited 39 young (20-35yrs) and 31 old (60-75yrs) untrained individuals to a 16 week progressive RT program, with a 32 week detraining/maintenance training period. In the maintenance period, one group was assigned to detraining, one group to a third of the initial volume via reduced training frequency (1 session, down from 3x/w), and one group to a ninth of the initial volume via reduced sets (1 set, down from 3) and training frequency (1 session, down from 3x/w). Following this, Bickel et al. (2011) found similar relative strength gains but greater hypertrophy gains in young compared to old, during the 16-week training program, and also an equally sustained enhancement of muscle performance during the detraining/maintenance phase, while maintenance of muscle mass gains required more frequent dosing in the old. Letocart et al. (2021) recruited 11 recreationally active men and 35 sedentary elderly men to a 12-week resistance program where the young exercised with a moderate-load training intervention corresponding to 55% of 1RM, while the old were randomly assigned to either moderate (55%) or high-load (80% of 1RM). They exercised three times a week, with three exercises for the lower extremities. Letocart et al. (2021) found that the old exercising with a moderate training intensity gained more m. quadriceps and m. triceps surae volume compared to the young, with no difference between old exercising with moderate- or high-intensity. Our findings align with Bickel et al. (2011) where greater hypertrophy gains were observed in young compared to old, and moderate-volume training being more beneficial in this regard, and none of these, or the aforementioned volume-manipulating studies have found low-volume to outperform moderate-volume in terms of skeletal muscle strength. This is a novel finding indeed, and could harken back to the pattern seen when contrasting Schoenfeld et al. (2017) and Krieger (2009), suggesting strength increases saturate at a lower training volume than hypertrophy.


<!-- P4: Ribosome biogenesis - RNA, UBF, cMyc, rnaseq? -->
Briefly, both UBF and c-Myc protein increased from baseline to week 3, however UBF content increased similarly in the old control, suggesting this was a general temporal effect rather than a training-specific response. On the contrary, the old control group had credibly lower c-Myc content compared to old intervention. Total RNA also increased in most groups including control, and differed by timing and not magnitude. The young increased primarily from baseline to week 3, and the old caught up by post, with no clear difference between age groups or intervention and control, and no volume condition effect. Lastly, the RNA-seq data revealed a largly age-independent training response dominated by up-regulation of ECM/collagen genes and down-regulation of RNA-processing/ribosome-biogenesis genes from baseline to post. The Age×time interaction is essentially null at the single-gene level, but GSEA shows old adults have a smaller-magnitude version of the same shared response (less RNA-splicing down-regulation, less angiogenesis/aerobic-respiration up-regulation). Training volume was impactful in the old (mitochondrial biogenesis up, contractile/translation genes down with more volume) but not at all in young. 

Findings from the present study suggests that ribosome biogenesis may be delayed rather than blunted in the elderly, as elderly reach close to the same levels of change as young, only at a later time point. The young group had the expected early rise following both moderate and low-volume exercise (19 and 16% respectively), which then declined somewhat at post (6 and 4%), a pattern consistent with previous findings from our lab [LIAN24, HAMMARSTROM]. While the elderly intervention group did not match this change after 3 weeks (mod = 8%, low = 10%), they achieved near similar increases at post (mod = 16%, low = 13%). These changes were credible at all times for both volume conditions in the young, however only at post for the elderly. It must also be noted that control had a similar baseline to post increase as old (13%), granted this was not a credible change, but the posterior probability suggested it to still be considered as moderate evidence, though not able to exclude a "no-difference" scenario. From baseline to week 3, the change in control was considered flat, at -1%. A possible explanation here could be timing of the strength tests, as post-strength testing was conducted three-four days prior to the biopsy - whereas at baseline biopsies were sampled before strength testing, and there were no strength testing at all around the week 3 biopsy sampling. Given that total RNA is quite sensitive to such stimuli [SOURCE ACUTE STUDIES], the strength testing alone may have caused the observed spike in total RNA in the control group, and does indeed present a methodological weakness of a poorly timed test. 

Changes in UBF and c-Myc protein matches the total RNA pattern quite well from baseline to week 3, with UBF increasing in all intervention groups, while c-Myc did not increase following low-volume exercise in the old intervention group. While c-Myc decreased in the old control group, content of UBF increased in a similar fashion to the intervention groups. Observed changes in protein content in the intervention group matches previous short-term/acute study findings [FIGUEIREDO16, LIAN24], and the fact that low-volume exercise did not induce a credible change in the old may further corroborate the narrative that increasing RT volume is more important for the elderly [LIXANDRAO24]. What does not quite add up in this story, is the increase of UBF content in the control group, paired with a decrease in c-Myc, since UBF is expected to be a downstream and training-specific target, triggered by c-Myc's transcriptional control [FIGUEIREDO16].

The RNA-seq pattern observed in the present study quite closely matches previous findings. An earlier metformin trial in older adults found progressive resistance training to significantly increase expression of genes involved in ECM remodelling and down-regulate genes in RNA-processing pathways [KULKARNI20], the same two dominant, opposite-direction gene sets observed in the present study. Recently, an aged-muscle reanalysis across modalities found that combined training and resistance training were mainly linked to ECM, collagen, adhesion, basement membrane, also similar to our results [YANG26]. Impaired transcriptional responses in mitochondrial, ECM and immune system genes have also been described as defining features of age-related anabolic resistance to resistance training [DEANE22], among these, baseline expression of genes related to oxidative phosphorylation was relatively lower in old compared to young, while genes related to activation of the immune system were relatively higher in the old, in the present study. These differences were not present at post, where young and old had a more similar profile than at baseline. 


<!-- P5: Glucose tolerance -->
Glucose tolerance improved more in the young compared to the old, specifically between 30 and 78 minutes after ingesting glucose. The only previous study including both young and old in a chronic RT intervention, found only nominal improvements in glucose tolerance in both groups, where elderly remained well below the young group [CRAIG89]. Notably, Craig et al. (1989) had fewer participants, and compared pre-post points rather than the full time frame of the OGTT like the present study. Chronic RT studies with old adults alone have found lowered 2h glucose and OGTT AUC compared to control after 8 weeks of RT (3x/week) [ANDERSSON17]; decreased fasting glucose and OGTT AUC (0-30min) after high-, low- and volume-matched load for 10 weeks [TSAI21]; decreased blood glucose, basal insulin, and HOMA-IR in postmenopausal women after 12 weeks of whole-body progressive RT [OLIVEIRA15]; and a decrease in HOMA-IR in non-diabetic elderly men compared to type 2 diabetic elderly men and control, after 12 weeks of RT (3x/week)[SHABKHIZ21]. Acute studies comparing single session volume effect have found reduced glucose AUC with RT, reduced fasting glucose only after higher-volume in young women [REED12], and improved oral glucose insulin sensitivity and glucose/insulin/c-peptide AUC in insulin resistant individuals after a high-volume session only [SILVA26]. A meta-analysis by Li et al. [LI21] investigated 12 RCTs with non-athletic and aged participants (60+), and found that population, training intensity, and duration all had significant effects on HOMA-IR, with largest effect sizes for high-intensity and long-term (>12 weeks) exercise in older adults without type 2 diabetes. In the same meta-analysis, they also found that moderate-intensity and short-term (<12 weeks) had a greater effect on HbA1c, particularly in people with type 2 diabetes [LI21]. On the contrary, Zhang et al. [ZHANG25] found more inconsistent evidence for high-intensity RT, with some long-term high-intensity trials failing to improve glycemia, HbA1c, or HOMA-IR. 

Taken together, the data suggest that chronic RT should improve glycemic markers in older adults, but the effect is modest and not universal. Chronic RT improved glucose/insulin/HOMA-IR in older adults in three separate studies [ANDERSSON17; TSAI21; OLIVEIRA15], with evidence from the meta-analysis by Li et al. (2021) supporting an effect, however small on average. This is corroborated by early findings from Craig et al. (1989) and more so the present study with a high resolution OGTT curve, that elderly do indeed respond in terms of improved glucose tolerance, however less than young adults undertaking the same chronic RT. Baseline metabolic health could be a moderator of the response, but in what direction is not clear. Chronic RT did not improve HOMA-IR in diabetic elderly men compared to non-diabetic elderly men, while both groups improved strength [SHABKHIZ21]. Acute RT, meanwhile, improved oral glucose sensitivity and glucose/insulin/C-peptide AUC only in the insulin resistant [SILVA26]. Notably, this may very well reflect chronic vs. acute mechanisms, but with the current findings its not a clear-cut "healthier responds more" picture. In the methodological perspective of the studies reviewed here, studies using fasting glucose/HOMA-IR [OLIVEIRA15; SHABKHIZ21; LI21] show less consistent findings and contradictory RT-intensity conclusions [LI21; ZHANG25], compared to studies using outcomes derived from the OGTT [ANDERSSON17; TSAI21]. Most of the methods used in these articles are collapsed to single-time point (fasting glucose/insulin, 2h glucose, HOMA-IR) or single summary statistics (OGTT AUC), which fails to capture the full window of post-prandial glucose clearance as the OGTT curve in the present study. This is important, since the difference between young and old in the present study would not have been detected by comparing for instance 2h glucose alone. Before 30 minutes, there was only a trend towards young having a larger improvement in glucose tolerance compared to the old, and after 78 min the we were no longer able to statistically distinguish any difference between the two intervention groups. The full OGTT curve also shows that not only has the old intervention group improved their glucose tolerance more than the old control group, but the difference remains credible to the last measured time point, whether the difference ends there or at a later time point however, we cannot tell.  

There might be an argument that the larger improvement observed in the young participants between 30 and 78 min is not meaningful, since the groups are statistically indistinguishable before 30 min and after 78; there's not a clear difference at the start or end of the test. However, there is evidence from cross-sectional/observational research that elevated 1-hour OGTT (>8.6 mmol/L) glucose identifies a higher-risk phenotype for future T2D and is independently associated with subclinical vascular damage and reduced insulin sensitivity/clearance, even in individuals who are indistinguishable from lower-risk individuals by standard fasting and 2h criteria [MARINI13; SCIACQUA12]. While this evidence concerns absolute 1h glucose level in cross-sectional cohorts rather than training-induced change, it indicates this region of the curve is not physiologically inert simply because it's invisible to standard fasting/2h criteria — though no comparable study has yet tested whether a training-induced improvement here confers the same protective association. It should also be noted here that while the appropriate RT volume could be an important lever [LI21, ZHANG25], this was not testable in the present study since the volume conditions were done within-participant.

Notably, there are considerable inter-individual variations in adaptations to RT, especially in the elderly, making prescription of an optimal RT program for different phenotypes difficult [@bamman_cluster_2007; @hammarstrom_benefits_2020-1; @hubal_variability_2005; @stec_effects_2015; @stec_ribosome_2016-1, @timmons_variability_2011]. While the underlying mechanisms of inter-individual variations to RT are not fully elucidated, differential manifestations of aging make the older population quite more heterogeneous than the young

This heterogeneity in physical function among the elderly is reflected by, perhaps most notably, the different presence of pathophysiological conditions such as insulin resistance, sarcopenia, and anabolic resistance [@fragala_resistance_2019; @hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016]. Whether anabolic resistance is a contributor to or a consequence of sarcopenia is uncertain, but the lower muscle protein synthesis (MPS) in the elderly following a session of RT or protein ingestion suggests that skeletal muscle in the elderly is less responsive to anabolic stimuli than in the young [@atherton_muscle_2012; @timmons_molecular_2016; @wall_aging_2015]. Baseline levels of MPS do not differ with age, however, the activity in proteins that influence MPS (e.g., mTOR) is elevated in fasted muscle from the elderly compared to young [@hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016; @markofski_effect_2015]. This discrepancy in mTOR activity is proposed to represent either a compensation to increased relative muscle loading due to decreased muscle mass with age, or dysregulation of the mTOR complex [@timmons_molecular_2016]. Further, likely as a consequence of altered mTOR regulation, ribosomal gene transcription and subsequently ribosome biogenesis is reduced in elderly [@chaillou_does_2023; @hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016], postulated to explain the anabolic resistance in the elderly in a recent study by Chaillou & Montiel-Rojas [@chaillou_does_2023].

Though occuring across age groups, the variation in ribosome biogenesis is proposed to be larger or more impactful among the elderly, substantiated by recent findings of impaired ribosome biogenesis in aging skeletal muscle [@chaillou_does_2023; @hodson_molecular_2019].
